title: Account deletion — Monzo
summary: Monzo requires the account balance (including Pots) to be brought to £0 before closure is allowed. The 'Close account' control sits at Profile > Settings > Close account, and the user confirms the closure and a reason in-app. After closing, Monzo emails a confirmation with a password-protected PDF bank statement (password sent separately via text). Full data deletion after closure is a separate, manual step requiring the user to email help@monzo.com or call, and can be done even without app access.
analysis: The zero-balance prerequisite functions as a real structural barrier (not just a warning) — closure is technically blocked until it's met — while data deletion is decoupled entirely from account closure and requires a second, manual support request, which most users likely never make.
steps: Withdraw all money from the main balance and any Pots until the total balance is £0
Open the Monzo app and go to Profile
Go to Settings > Close account
Tap 'Close Account' and confirm the decision
Optionally select/provide a reason for closing
Receive an email confirmation with a password-protected PDF statement (password sent via SMS)
Separately email help@monzo.com or call to request full data deletion, if desired

title: Account deletion — Wise
summary: Wise's help center instructs users to first withdraw all balances (Jars, Stocks, Interest, multi-currency balances) individually before closing, and to download any statements/receipts needed since they won't be accessible after. Closure is initiated via the account name menu > Settings > Close account, which the site notes does not close the account immediately — the user is walked through further steps rather than a single confirmation click.
analysis: The explicit warning that clicking 'Close account' does not immediately close it, combined with the requirement to manually zero out every currency balance one at a time, signals a deliberately multi-stage flow designed to force users to fully unwind their account state before Wise will let go of it.
steps: Withdraw money from every currency balance, Jar, and Stocks/Interest holding individually
Cancel or complete any pending transactions and card payments
Download any transfer receipts or balance statements needed for records
Go to the account name menu (top corner) > Settings
Select 'Close account'
Follow the additional guided steps presented (closure is not immediate on clicking the option)

title: Account deletion — Netflix
summary: Netflix's self-service flow (profile icon > Account > Cancel Membership) only cancels the paid subscription; it does not delete the account or its data. Netflix's own help guidance states there is no self-service 'delete account' button, and full account/data deletion must be requested via live chat, phone contact, or emailing privacy@netflix.com. Netflix separately confirms that a canceled-but-undeleted account is automatically deleted after a period of inactivity.
analysis: Netflix is a clean example of the 'cancel' and 'delete' actions being entirely different, non-overlapping flows — one is a one-click self-service button, the other requires contacting a human — which is easy for a user to miss since cancellation feels like it should be the end of the story.
steps: Sign in and click the profile icon in the top right
Select 'Account' from the dropdown menu
Under Membership & Billing, click 'Cancel Membership' (this stops billing at the end of the current cycle, it does not delete the account)
To fully delete the account/data instead of waiting, contact Netflix via live chat or phone, or email privacy@netflix.com
Separately, go to netflix.com/password and select 'Sign out of all devices' for security after cancelling

title: Account deletion — Spotify
summary: Spotify requires web (not mobile app) access to close an account: users sign in at support.spotify.com, go to Account > 'I want to close my account,' confirm account details, and accept the loss of playlists/library/subscription. Premium subscribers must cancel Premium first, as a paid plan can't be cancelled through this flow directly. A confirmation link is then emailed, and the account remains reactivatable for 7 days before permanent closure and anonymization proceeds.
analysis: Requiring desktop/web access specifically (mobile app has no deletion path) is an unusual and easy-to-miss friction point for a product that is overwhelmingly used on mobile.
steps: Cancel any active Premium subscription first, if applicable
Go to support.spotify.com on a desktop/web browser and sign in
Navigate to Account > 'I want to close my account'
Confirm account details and acknowledge the consequences (loss of playlists, library, subscriptions; username gets locked)
Wait for a confirmation email containing a closure link
Click the link to complete closure; account can still be reactivated within 7 days
After 7 days, the account can no longer be reactivated and data deletion/anonymization begins (fully anonymized within 14-30 days)

title: Account deletion — Discord
summary: Discord's deletion flow is in User Settings > My Account > 'Delete Account,' which requires re-entering the account password and, if enabled, completing MFA. Users must first transfer ownership of, or delete, any servers they own before the option becomes available. Once confirmed, the account enters a stated 14-day pending-deletion window during which logging back in cancels the deletion; Discord support states it cannot expedite this waiting period and the deletion is irreversible once it completes.
analysis: Discord explicitly refuses to let its own support team speed up the waiting period even on request, which is a stronger and more unusual commitment to the cooling-off window than most companies make.
steps: Transfer ownership of, or delete, any Discord servers the account owns
Open User Settings (cogwheel icon) and go to the My Account tab
Select 'Delete Account' at the bottom of the page
Enter the account password to confirm
Complete multi-factor authentication if MFA is enabled
Account enters a pending-deletion period (around 14 days) during which logging in cancels the deletion
After the waiting period elapses, the account is permanently and irreversibly deleted

title: Account deletion — Instagram
summary: Deletion is nested inside Meta's Accounts Center: Profile > Menu > Settings and privacy > Accounts Center > Personal details > Account ownership and control > Deactivation or deletion, then select the account and 'Delete account.' The user picks a reason and re-enters their password before confirming. Instagram documents a 30-day grace period during which logging back in cancels the deletion request; after 30 days the profile, photos, videos, comments, likes and followers are stated to be permanently deleted and unrecoverable, and the export-your-information tool is no longer available afterward.
analysis: Routing account deletion through the shared cross-app 'Accounts Center' (rather than Instagram's own settings) reflects Meta's platform-wide identity consolidation, and buries a fairly high-stakes, hard-to-reverse action several menu layers deep.
steps: Go to Profile > Menu > Settings and privacy > Accounts Center
Tap Personal details > Account ownership and control > Deactivation or deletion
Select the account to delete and tap 'Delete account' > Continue
Select a reason for deleting from the dropdown
Enter the account password when prompted
Tap 'Delete [username]' to confirm
Account enters a 30-day grace period; logging back in during this window cancels the deletion
After 30 days, profile and all associated data are permanently deleted

title: Account deletion — LinkedIn
summary: LinkedIn's 'Close account' option is under Settings & Privacy > Account management, requiring the user to select a reason and re-enter their account password to confirm. LinkedIn's help documentation states the profile is deactivated and most data (recommendations, endorsements, messages, connections) is deleted, with reactivation possible if done within 14 days; after that, closure is treated as permanent and information cannot be recovered. Users with Premium, Groups ownership, or third-party-linked login must resolve those first.
analysis: LinkedIn frames closure as immediate profile removal with only account reactivation as the safety net (14 days), rather than describing a delayed data-purge schedule — a subtly different (and more account-centric than data-centric) framing than Instagram's or Discord's grace-period language.
steps: Click the 'Me' icon on the LinkedIn homepage and select Settings & Privacy
Go to Account preferences > Account management
Click 'Close account' and then 'Continue'
Select a reason for closing and click 'Next'
Enter the account password and click 'Done'
Account can be reactivated by logging back in within 14 days; after that it is treated as permanently closed

title: Account deletion — GitHub
summary: GitHub requires prerequisite cleanup before deletion is allowed: sole organization owners must transfer ownership or delete the org, and members of other organizations must first remove themselves. The self-service control is at Settings > Account > 'Delete account' (bottom of page), and GitHub's docs require the user to type their username/email and a specific confirmation phrase in a 'Make sure you want to do this' dialog. GitHub states deletion is immediate and irreversible — content cannot be restored afterward.
analysis: The typed confirmation-phrase pattern (rather than a simple password re-entry or single confirm click) is a friction mechanism specifically aimed at preventing accidental clicks on an irreversible, immediate-effect action, which contrasts with the multi-day cooling-off approach most consumer social apps use instead.
steps: Ensure the account is not the sole owner of any organization (transfer ownership or delete the org first)
Remove yourself from any other organizations you belong to
Make a copy of any repositories, private forks, wikis, issues, and pull requests you want to keep
Go to Settings in the top-right profile menu, then click 'Account' in the left sidebar
Scroll to the 'Delete account' section at the bottom and click 'Delete your account'
In the confirmation dialog, type your username or email, then type the required confirmation phrase
Confirm — deletion is immediate and cannot be undone by GitHub

title: Account deletion — Notion
summary: Notion's flow is Settings (sidebar) > {your name} > 'Delete my account,' which opens a confirmation window listing which workspaces will be deleted alongside the account. The user must manually type their account email to proceed, then click 'Permanently delete account and {#} workspaces.' Notion's help center states deletion is permanent going forward, but notes the company keeps database backups and may be able to restore a snapshot of content from within the prior 30 days on request via support.
analysis: Notion is unusual in publicly documenting an informal post-deletion recovery path (backup-based restoration within 30 days via a support request) even though the deletion action itself is framed to the user as permanent — a hedge most companies don't openly advertise.
steps: Go to Settings in the left sidebar, then click your name
Select 'Delete my account'
Review the confirmation window listing which workspace(s) will be deleted along with the account
Manually type your account email to confirm
Click 'Permanently delete account and {#} workspaces'
(Optional, after the fact) contact Notion support within 30 days to request restoration from backup if deletion was accidental

title: Account deletion — Uber
summary: Uber's rider deletion path runs through its Privacy Center: in-app via Account icon > Manage Uber account > Privacy & Data > Privacy Center > Account Deletion, or directly at myprivacy.uber.com. The flow requires identity verification via a one-time code sent to the phone/email on file, and blocks deletion if there is an outstanding payment balance. After the request, the account is immediately deactivated but only permanently deleted after 30 days (during which unused credits/promotions/rewards would be forfeited); signing back in within that window restores the account.
analysis: Requiring a live one-time verification code (rather than just a password) to initiate deletion is a meaningfully stronger identity check than most consumer apps use for this action, likely reflecting Uber's need to prevent account takeover in a service tied to real-world payments and location.
steps: Ensure there is no outstanding payment balance on the account
Open the Uber app, tap the Account icon, and select 'Manage Uber account'
Go to Privacy & Data > Privacy Center
Scroll to and tap 'Account Deletion' (or go to myprivacy.uber.com and log in directly)
Follow the on-screen prompts and enter the one-time verification code sent via email or phone
Account is immediately deactivated; signing in again within 30 days restores it
After 30 days with no sign-in, the account and any remaining credits/promotions are permanently deleted

title: Account deletion — Airbnb
summary: Airbnb documents two distinct actions: 'Deactivate' (Menu > Account settings > Login & security > Deactivate, choosing a reason and confirming), which cancels current reservations under the applicable cancellation policy and can be reversed by contacting Airbnb; and 'Delete,' reached via Account > Privacy, which Airbnb states requires identity verification before the request is accepted. Once a deletion request is processed, Airbnb states personal information is permanently erased except what it is legally required to retain, and the action cannot be reversed or reactivated — a new account would be needed to return.
analysis: Airbnb draws an unusually sharp, explicitly documented line between 'deactivate' (reversible, support can undo it) and 'delete' (identity-verified, permanent, no support recourse), which is a clearer two-tier model than most companies that blur cancellation and deletion together.
steps: For deactivation: go to Menu > Account settings > Login & security, click Deactivate under Account
Choose a reason for deactivating and click Continue, then click 'Deactivate account'
(Reservations as host or guest are cancelled per the applicable cancellation policy)
For full deletion instead: go to Account > Privacy and submit a deletion request
Complete Airbnb's identity verification before the request is accepted
Once processed, personal information is permanently erased except legally-required retentions; the account cannot be reactivated

title: Account deletion — PayPal
summary: PayPal requires the account balance to be removed and any account limitations or unresolved issues (e.g. open disputes) resolved before closure is permitted. On desktop, the path is the Settings menu (icon near Log out) > Account options > 'Close your account' link > 'Close account' button; on mobile it's profile icon > Settings > 'Close your account.' PayPal states that once closed, an account cannot be reopened.
analysis: The blanket 'cannot be reopened' policy is stricter than most of the other companies surveyed, several of which offer 7-30 day reactivation windows — PayPal's payments/liability context likely makes it unwilling to let a closed account come back to life.
steps: Withdraw or transfer any remaining balance out of the account
Resolve any account limitations, open disputes, or unauthorized-payment reports
On desktop: open the Settings menu (icon near Log out), go to Account options, click 'Close your account'
On mobile: tap the profile icon, go to Settings, tap 'Close your account' at the bottom
Click/tap 'Close account' to confirm
Account is closed and, per PayPal, cannot be reopened afterward

title: Identity verification — Revolut
summary: Revolut requires users to photograph a government-issued ID (passport, driver's license, national ID, or state ID) via the in-app camera, then complete a biometric check consisting of a live selfie, facial scan, or short video matched against the ID; in some cases users are also asked to photograph the ID held next to their face. Revolut states review usually takes up to 1 business day but can take up to 7 business days in some cases. Documented rejection causes include document glare/cropping, poor selfie lighting, an obstructed face, or extra people visible in frame.
analysis: Revolut publishes an unusually granular public troubleshooting library of specific selfie rejection reasons (lighting, hats, multiple people in frame) rather than a single generic FAQ, suggesting verification failure and resubmission is common enough to warrant dedicated support content.
steps: Open the app and start the identity verification flow
Select ID type: passport, driver's license, national ID, or state ID
Photograph the front (and back if applicable) of the document using the in-app camera
Complete a live selfie, facial scan, or short video selfie
If prompted, take an additional photo holding the ID next to your face
Submit for automated and manual review (up to 1 business day, up to 7 in some cases)
Receive approval or rejection; if rejected, resubmit following the specific corrective guidance shown

title: Identity verification — Monzo
summary: When opening an account, Monzo has new customers photograph an ID document (passport or driving licence recommended) and record a short (~5-second) video selfie repeating a scripted phrase including their name, which is compared to the ID photo using facial recognition and document-authenticity checks. Monzo states the capture itself usually takes a minute or two, though full verification checks can take up to 48 hours, during which the account may be restricted. Customers who can't record video with audio are offered an alternative way to provide the phrase.
analysis: The scripted spoken phrase, rather than a silent selfie or head-turn gesture, is a distinctive liveness design — it doubles as both an anti-spoofing signal and an audible identity claim, which Monzo's own blog frames as a deliberate workaround for being a branch-less bank rather than a vendor-imposed requirement.
steps: Sign up in the Monzo app and reach the identity verification step
Take a photo of an ID document (passport or driving licence recommended)
Record a short video selfie repeating a scripted phrase that includes your name
System runs document authenticity checks and facial recognition matching video to ID photo
Account is typically created immediately; further checks continue in the background for up to 48 hours
If unable to record video with audio, contact support for an alternative method
If checks fail, account access may be temporarily frozen pending resubmission

title: Identity verification — Coinbase
summary: Coinbase requires new users to submit a valid government ID showing legal name, date of birth, and address/country, plus a selfie or short video captured via the in-app camera. Coinbase names Onfido as the vendor that compares facial scan data from the selfie against the ID photo and checks the document for authenticity and tampering. Coinbase states review status is typically returned within 24 hours; documented failure causes include glare, expired documents, and name/address mismatches with the account profile.
analysis: Coinbase is one of the few companies reviewed that explicitly names its verification vendor (Onfido) in public disclosures rather than keeping it generic, likely reflecting its obligations as a regulated money transmitter to disclose subprocessors handling biometric data.
steps: Enter personal information (legal name, date of birth, address) in-app
Choose ID document type and capture front/back with device camera
Capture a live selfie or short video following on-screen prompts
Onfido compares facial data to the ID photo and checks document authenticity
Receive verification result, typically within 24 hours
If verification fails, follow troubleshooting guidance (lighting, validity, name mismatch) and resubmit

title: Identity verification — Wise
summary: Wise verifies identity by having users upload a photo of an accepted ID (passport photo page, national ID card, or photo driver's licence) plus a separate live selfie photo of their face, and in some cases a proof-of-address document or a photo of the user holding their ID. Wise's help center describes using facial recognition to match the selfie to the ID document. No specific third-party verification vendor is named in Wise's public help articles.
analysis: Wise's documentation is notably conditional and country-dependent ("usually," "may also ask") compared to peers, suggesting the exact document set varies by jurisdiction — a reflection of Wise's fragmented, country-by-country licensing structure rather than one uniform global flow.
steps: Enter name and date of birth matching official records
Select and photograph/scan an accepted ID document (passport, national ID, or driver's licence)
Take a separate live selfie photo of your face
If requested, provide a proof-of-address document or a photo holding the ID
Submit documents through the Wise app or web account
Wise reviews and confirms identity, requesting additional documents if information doesn't match

title: Identity verification — Kraken
summary: Kraken uses a tiered verification system where higher tiers unlock greater limits and features; verification requires a government-issued ID and, depending on tier/country, a face photo and/or a proof-of-address document dated within the last three months. Kraken's support documentation states face photos are sent to Persona for the liveness step, instructing users to avoid hats/sunglasses, use good lighting, and follow on-screen prompts to turn their head.
analysis: Kraken gates verification depth by account tier rather than requiring full document-plus-liveness KYC upfront for every user — a notably different design from Coinbase/Binance's more uniform onboarding, deferring the heaviest burden until a user wants higher limits.
steps: Create account and select the verification tier to pursue
Submit government-issued ID document (front/back as required)
Provide a proof-of-address document if address isn't auto-confirmed, dated within 3 months
Complete face photo/liveness step (processed via Persona): center face, remove hats/glasses, turn head per prompts
Submit for review
Receive tier upgrade on approval, or troubleshooting guidance if a document/photo is rejected

title: Identity verification — Robinhood
summary: Robinhood can prompt users for a "three-point selfie" (face, shoulders, and ID all visible) or a photo of the front and back of a government ID as one of several step-up verification methods — alongside device approval, SMS code, or bank verification — triggered by new-device logins or account changes. Robinhood's disclosures name Persona as the vendor that may compare the selfie to the government ID on file, noting collected biometric data is retained per financial regulations.
analysis: Robinhood applies selfie/ID verification primarily as an ongoing, risk-triggered step-up security control rather than a single mandatory onboarding gate — closer to a continuous authentication pattern than the one-time KYC-at-signup pattern used elsewhere on this list.
steps: A trigger event (new device login, account change, or suspicious activity) prompts a "Verify it's you" request
User is offered or assigned a verification method: device approval, SMS code, bank verification, three-point selfie, or ID photo
For selfie: position face, shoulders, and (if requested) ID card in frame in a well-lit space without glasses/hats
Persona compares the selfie to the ID on file
Access is granted immediately on match, or flagged for further review/support contact on mismatch

title: Identity verification — PayPal
summary: To satisfy its Customer Identification Program (CIP), PayPal offers two paths: a mobile facial biometric flow where users scan the front and back of a government photo ID and take a matching selfie, or a desktop flow where users upload a photo/scan of an ID plus a proof-of-address document. PayPal states document review is typically completed within 2 business days, though it can take longer.
analysis: PayPal runs two structurally different verification paths — automated camera-based biometrics on mobile versus manual document upload on desktop — a split design that likely reflects identity checks being retrofitted onto an older, established payments platform rather than built mobile-first from the ground up.
steps: Log in and open the "Confirm your Identity" prompt (via notification or account restriction notice)
Choose method: mobile facial biometric verification or desktop document upload
Mobile path: scan front and back of government photo ID, then take a matching selfie
Desktop path: upload photo/scan of ID and a proof-of-address document
Submit for review
PayPal reviews within about 2 business days and notifies the user of the outcome or requests more documentation

title: Identity verification — Stripe Connect (platform seller onboarding)
summary: Platforms built on Stripe Connect use Stripe-hosted Connect Onboarding to collect seller/connected-account identity information, dynamically requesting a scan of a government-issued ID and/or a proof-of-address document depending on the account's country, business type, and required capabilities; platforms can additionally embed Stripe Identity's document-plus-selfie check for stronger verification. Stripe's documentation frames the exact requirements as configurable per integrating platform rather than one fixed universal flow.
analysis: This is the clearest example on this list of identity verification delivered as infrastructure rather than a single company's product decision — the document/selfie requirements a seller actually sees are set by whichever marketplace integrates Stripe, so the visible user flow varies by client even though the backend verification technology is shared.
steps: Seller starts onboarding on a Stripe-powered platform and is redirected to Stripe-hosted Connect Onboarding
Form dynamically requests information based on country, business type, and required capabilities
Seller uploads a scan of a government-issued ID and, if required, a proof-of-address document
If the platform has enabled the Stripe Identity add-on, seller also completes a selfie check matched against the ID
Stripe verifies the submitted information and documents
Seller is redirected back to the platform with verification complete, pending, or requiring more information

title: Identity verification — DoorDash (Dasher onboarding)
summary: Before dashing, applicants upload a current government-issued ID and take a selfie matched against it via Persona's selfie biometrics, alongside a separate criminal- and motor-vehicle-history background check run through third-party provider Checkr using their Social Security Number. DoorDash also runs recurring real-time selfie re-checks on active Dashers, and suspends the account from dashing if identity can't be reverified.
analysis: DoorDash layers two separately-vendored checks — a one-time criminal/background screen via Checkr and an ongoing biometric identity check via Persona that continues after onboarding — a heavier, more continuous verification burden than most consumer fintech apps that verify only once at signup.
steps: Submit application with government ID upload during signup
Take a selfie via in-app camera to be matched against the ID (Persona)
Provide SSN and consent for a background check through Checkr (criminal history + motor vehicle record)
Wait for background check status (Pending, Clear, or Consider), typically 5-7 business days
Once cleared, begin dashing
Periodically prompted for real-time selfie re-verification while active
If a selfie fails to match or identity can't be reverified, the Dasher account is suspended pending resolution

title: Identity verification — Uber (driver Real-Time ID Check)
summary: Uber's Real-Time ID Check periodically prompts drivers and couriers to take a live selfie in the app, which is matched against the verified profile photo on file; Uber's engineering blog states it used Microsoft's Face API to perform the comparison. A match lets the driver continue accepting trips; a mismatch results in a temporary block from the platform while Uber investigates, and photos of photos/screens are explicitly rejected.
analysis: Uber's flow is unusual for relying purely on selfie-to-profile-photo matching with no repeated document re-scan — identity is established once via the profile photo and then continuously re-verified against that baseline, a lighter-weight but higher-frequency pattern than the one-time document-plus-selfie flows used at onboarding elsewhere on this list.
steps: App prompts driver/courier at intervals to verify identity before going online
Driver takes a real-time selfie using the in-app camera
Microsoft Face API compares the live selfie to the driver's on-file verified profile photo
On match, driver is allowed to go online and accept trips
On mismatch, driver is temporarily blocked from the app while Uber investigates
Driver can submit a selfie for manual review by a support specialist if needed

title: Identity verification — Airbnb
summary: Airbnb may require users to submit a photo of a government-issued ID (national ID card, driver's license, passport, state ID, tribal ID, or residence permit depending on location) plus a selfie matched against the ID photo. Users can consent to automated facial recognition matching, or opt instead for manual photo review by an Airbnb team member; Airbnb states the ID and selfie are not shared with other hosts or guests.
analysis: Airbnb is one of the few platforms here that documents an explicit consent-based fork away from automated facial recognition toward human manual review — an opt-out most other companies on this list don't publicly offer or disclose.
steps: User is prompted to verify identity (e.g., before booking or hosting)
Select the ID document type accepted in their country and photograph it
Take a selfie to be matched against the ID photo
Choose to consent to automated facial recognition matching, or opt for manual review instead
Automated system (or human reviewer) compares selfie to ID photo
User is notified once verification is complete; ID and selfie are not visible to other users

title: Identity verification — Binance
summary: Binance requires users to upload a government-issued ID (e.g., passport or driver's license), including front and back photos where applicable, followed by a liveness check requiring a live, video-style capture (center face, follow on-screen prompts, no hats/glasses/filters) rather than a static photo. Binance states submitted KYC documents are typically reviewed within 48 hours.
analysis: Binance's requirement of a video-style liveness capture rather than a static selfie is one of the stricter liveness implementations among the crypto exchanges reviewed here, likely reflecting the heavier regulatory and fraud/deepfake scrutiny global crypto exchanges face.
steps: Enter personal information and select country of residence
Choose ID document type and photograph front and back using device camera
Complete liveness check: center face in frame, follow on-screen prompts, no hats/glasses/filters
Submit documents for review
Receive verification result, typically within 48 hours
If verification fails, review the checklist (image quality, cropping, glare) and resubmit via Help Center or Support Chat
